lead: A Carnot engine is a reversible heat engine that takes heat Q<sub>H</sub> from a hot reservoir at T<sub>H</sub>, rejects heat Q<sub>C</sub> to a cold reservoir at T<sub>C</sub>, and returns to its starting state. Every step is reversible, so it gives the best efficiency possible between those two temperatures. Real power plants, refrigerators and heat pumps are compared with this limit. The Carnot theorems and the thermodynamic temperature scale turn that comparison into a precise tool for calculating temperatures and efficiencies.
prereq: You need: the second-law statements and the engine energy balance of heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps, the ideal-gas isothermal and adiabatic relations from PVT behaviour and equations of state, and the meaning of a reversible process from the first-law chapters.

sections.h3: The four Carnot steps on an ideal gas

blocks.text: Take n moles of ideal gas in a piston–cylinder. The gas is the working fluid. The cycle has two isothermal steps at the reservoir temperatures and two adiabatic steps that change temperature. All steps are reversible.

items: 1 → 2: isothermal expansion at T<sub>H</sub>. The gas takes Q<sub>H</sub> from the hot reservoir and does work. For an ideal gas, Q<sub>H</sub> = n R T<sub>H</sub> ln(V₂/V₁); n is moles, R is the gas constant, V is volume.
2 → 3: adiabatic expansion from T<sub>H</sub> to T<sub>C</sub>. Q = 0, so the gas cools while doing work.
3 → 4: isothermal compression at T<sub>C</sub>. Work is done on the gas and it rejects Q<sub>C</sub> to the cold reservoir. Q<sub>C</sub> = n R T<sub>C</sub> ln(V₃/V₄) as a positive magnitude.
4 → 1: adiabatic compression from T<sub>C</sub> back to T<sub>H</sub>. Q = 0, and the gas returns to its starting state.

blocks.text: For a reversible adiabatic step of an ideal gas TV<sup>γ−1</sup> is constant (γ = C<sub>P</sub>/C<sub>V</sub>), so T<sub>H</sub> V₂<sup>γ−1</sup> = T<sub>C</sub> V₃<sup>γ−1</sup> and T<sub>H</sub> V₁<sup>γ−1</sup> = T<sub>C</sub> V₄<sup>γ−1</sup>. Dividing one by the other gives (V₂/V₁) = (V₃/V₄), so the two logarithms are equal. Divide the heat magnitudes: Q<sub>H</sub>/Q<sub>C</sub> = T<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>C</sub>. This ratio is the key result; it does not depend on n or R.

blocks.where: Q<sub>H</sub> is heat taken from the hot reservoir; Q<sub>C</sub> is heat rejected to the cold reservoir, both in kJ; T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub> are absolute temperatures in kelvin.

sections.h3: Carnot theorems and the thermodynamic temperature scale

blocks.text: First Carnot theorem: no engine working between two fixed reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine between the same two reservoirs. Second Carnot theorem: all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, whatever the working fluid. The proof idea is a pair of coupled engines. If a claimed engine were better, reverse the reversible one and the pair would move heat from cold to hot with no net work input, which the Clausius statement forbids (see the second-law statements).

For any reversible engine, the ratio Q<sub>H</sub>/Q<sub>C</sub> depends only on the two reservoir temperatures. This lets us define the thermodynamic temperature scale: T<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>C</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/Q<sub>C</sub> for a reversible engine. The scale needs one fixed value. It was fixed by giving the triple point of water exactly 273.16 K; since 2019 the kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant, k<sub>B</sub> = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K, and the triple point stays at 273.16 K within measurement error. Then the Carnot efficiency follows from the first law, W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>, and the definition.

blocks.where: η<sub>C</sub> is the Carnot efficiency; W is net work output; Q<sub>H</sub> is heat taken from the hot reservoir; Q<sub>C</sub> is heat rejected; T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub> are absolute temperatures in kelvin.

blocks.text: For the reversed cycle, the same engine becomes a refrigerator or heat pump. Its coefficient of performance (COP) is the useful heat divided by work input.

blocks.where: COP<sub>R</sub> is the refrigerator COP; Q<sub>C</sub> is heat removed from the cold space; W is work input; T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub> are absolute temperatures.
COP<sub>HP</sub> is the heat-pump COP; Q<sub>H</sub> is heat delivered to the hot space.

sections.h3: What the efficiency limit tells you

blocks.text: The formula η<sub>C</sub> = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> has three practical readings. Raising T<sub>H</sub> raises η<sub>C</sub>. Lowering T<sub>C</sub> raises η<sub>C</sub>. Making T<sub>C</sub> approach 0 K makes η<sub>C</sub> approach 1, but no real cold sink is at absolute zero, so 100 % is impossible.

A real steam plant has irreversibilities: friction, finite temperature differences, and heat leaks. Its efficiency is below the Carnot value between the same boiler and condenser temperatures; the gap is lost work (see lost work and ideal work). Real Rankine cycles are treated in steam power plant cycles, and vapour-compression cycles in refrigeration and liquefaction.

The same limit applies to refrigerators. To get a large COP<sub>R</sub>, keep T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>C</sub> small. A domestic refrigerator in a hot room therefore works harder than the same refrigerator in a cool room. This is the Carnot limit in everyday use.

examples.question: A Carnot engine works between a hot reservoir at 600 K and a cold reservoir at 300 K. It takes 1000 kJ from the hot reservoir per cycle. Find the Carnot efficiency η, the net work W, and the heat rejected Q<sub>C</sub>.
steps: T<sub>H</sub> = 600 K, T<sub>C</sub> = 300 K, Q<sub>H</sub> = 1000 kJ.
Energy balance: Q<sub>H</sub> = W + Q<sub>C</sub>, so Q<sub>C</sub> = 1000 − 500 = 500 kJ. Check: Q<sub>C</sub>/Q<sub>H</sub> = 0.5 = T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>.
examples.answer: η = 50 %, W = 500 kJ, and Q<sub>C</sub> = 500 kJ.
examples.check:
TH = 600.0
TC = 300.0
QH = 1000.0
eta = 1 - TC/TH
W = eta * QH
QC = QH - W
print(eta)
print(W)
print(QC)

examples.question: A reversible engine works between a hot body at an unknown temperature T and a bath at the triple point of water (273.16 K). Per cycle it takes 500 kJ from the hot body and rejects 250 kJ to the bath. Find T on the thermodynamic scale and the engine efficiency.
steps: For a reversible engine the thermodynamic scale gives T/T<sub>tp</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/Q<sub>C</sub>.
η = 1 − Q<sub>C</sub>/Q<sub>H</sub> = 1 − 250/500 = 0.50; the same value as 1 − 273.16/546.32.
No thermometer fluid was used: the temperature comes from heat ratios alone.

traps: Using Celsius temperatures in η = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>. Use kelvin; 27 °C and 327 °C are 300 K and 600 K, not 27 and 327.
Using η = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> for a real engine. That formula is for a reversible Carnot engine; a real engine needs its actual Q<sub>H</sub> and Q<sub>C</sub>.
Treating Q<sub>C</sub>/Q<sub>H</sub> = T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> as true for every engine. The ratio is fixed only for a reversible cycle between those reservoirs.
Thinking a COP above 1 breaks the second law. A refrigerator COP of 9 or a heat-pump COP of 15 is allowed; efficiency η is the quantity that cannot exceed 1.

Writing W = Q<sub>C</sub> − Q<sub>H</sub> for a refrigerator. Work input is positive when W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>, because heat delivered to the hot side is larger than heat removed from the cold side.

quiz.a: No engine between two reservoirs is more efficient than a reversible engine between the same reservoirs; all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have equal efficiency, independent of the working fluid.

quiz.q: Why must the efficiency of any real engine between 600 K and 300 K be below 50 %?
quiz.a: The Carnot value is 1 − 300/600 = 0.50. Irreversibilities generate entropy, so a real engine delivers less work than the reversible engine for the same heat input. A claim above 50 % would violate the second law.

quiz.q: A Carnot refrigerator works between T<sub>C</sub> = 270 K and T<sub>H</sub> = 300 K. Find COP<sub>R</sub>. If it removes 270 kJ from the cold space, find the work input.
quiz.a: COP<sub>R</sub> = T<sub>C</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>C</sub>) = 270/(300 − 270) = 9. W = Q<sub>C</sub>/COP<sub>R</sub> = 270/9 = 30 kJ. Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W = 300 kJ.

quiz.q: A Carnot engine between 500 K and 300 K takes 800 kJ from the hot reservoir. Find η, W and Q<sub>C</sub>.
An inventor claims an engine takes 1000 kJ from 600 K, rejects 450 kJ to 300 K, and delivers the rest as work. Test the claim.
quiz.a: Claimed efficiency = (1000 − 450)/1000 = 0.55. Carnot limit = 1 − 300/600 = 0.50. The claim exceeds the limit, so no engine between these reservoirs can do it.

quiz.q: What is the thermodynamic temperature scale, and why is a reversible engine needed to define it?
quiz.a: It defines the absolute temperature ratio by T<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>C</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/Q<sub>C</sub>. A reversible engine is needed so the heat ratio depends only on the two reservoir temperatures, not on irreversibility or the working fluid.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Carnot limit is the reference for exergy analysis, where every real plant is measured against a reversible path to the environment. Finite-time thermodynamics asks how fast a cycle can run before irreversibility eats the gain. Search for "finite-time thermodynamics" and "ITS-90 temperature scale".
